nameStory: Wilson's Snipe honors Alexander Wilson, often called the 'Father of American Ornithology,' who described many North American birds in the early 1800s. The word 'snipe' comes from the Old Norse 'snipa,' referring to the bird's long, pointed bill that resembles a snipe or pointed tool.
description: Wilson's Snipe is a small, chunky shorebird about the size of a robin, with a body built like a football with legs. Its most striking feature is an incredibly long, straight bill that looks almost comically oversized for its compact body. The bird's plumage is beautifully patterned with rich browns, buffs, and blacks in intricate stripes and bars that provide perfect camouflage among marsh grasses and muddy shores. Despite being a shorebird, you're more likely to find it probing soft mud in wetlands than walking along ocean beaches.

idTips.label: Extremely Long Bill
idTips.description: The bill is nearly as long as the head and body combined, perfectly straight, and dark-colored - looks like a knitting needle stuck on a small bird

idTips.label: Striped Head Pattern
idTips.description: Bold dark stripes run lengthwise over a buff-colored head, creating a distinctive racing-stripe pattern that's visible even from a distance

idTips.label: Zigzag Flight
idTips.description: When flushed, flies in a distinctive erratic zigzag pattern while making a harsh 'scaipe' call - looks like it can't decide which direction to go

idTips.label: Stocky Body Shape
idTips.description: Short neck and legs with a plump, rounded body that sits low to the ground - built more like a small chicken than a typical long-legged shorebird

idTips.label: Camouflaged Plumage
idTips.description: Intricate pattern of browns, blacks, and buffs in stripes and bars that make the bird nearly invisible when motionless among dead grasses and marsh vegetation

habitat: Wilson's Snipes prefer soft, muddy areas where they can easily probe for food - think marshy edges of ponds, wet meadows, boggy areas, and muddy shores of slow-moving streams. They love spots where grasses and sedges provide cover, especially areas that stay damp even during dry spells. You'll often find them in places where your boots would sink slightly into the squishy ground.

seasonality.spring: Peak migration time when snipes are most visible, often performing dramatic aerial courtship displays with haunting winnowing sounds made by air rushing through their tail feathers.
seasonality.summer: Breeding birds become secretive and harder to spot, staying hidden in dense marsh vegetation while tending to nests and young on the ground.
seasonality.fall: Migration period when numbers increase again, and birds may be found in a wider variety of wet habitats as they move south.
seasonality.winter: Some hardy individuals may overwinter in spring-fed areas that don't freeze, but most have departed for warmer regions by late fall.

funFact: Wilson's Snipe can actually bend the tip of their bill while it's buried in mud - the tip is flexible and packed with nerve endings, allowing them to feel around underground and grab worms without ever seeing them, like having super-sensitive fingers at the end of their nose!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with woodcock, but Wilson's Snipe has a much longer, thinner bill and prefers open marshy areas rather than woodcock's wooded habitats. Remember: Snipe = swamp, Woodcock = woods.
contextualKnowledge: This species was considered the same as the Common Snipe found in Europe until 2003, when scientists determined they were actually separate species. The phrase 'snipe hunt' comes from the real difficulty of hunting these birds due to their excellent camouflage and erratic flight pattern.
compareHints: Wilson's Snipe is the only true snipe species regularly found in New England. Compared to other long-billed shorebirds in the region like dowitchers, Wilson's Snipe is much more secretive, prefers freshwater marshes over coastal areas, and has that distinctive stocky build rather than the longer legs and necks of most shorebirds.
